{"passages":[{"reference":"1.5","text":"What, then, must I do but this? I will travel to Egypt, befriend the hierophants and prophets of the inner sanctuaries, and, after searching for and finding a magician, persuade him with a great deal of money to summon up a soul—the practice called necromancy—while I inquire as though about some particular matter. But my inquiry will be about learning whether the soul is immortal. I will know the soul’s answer, that it is immortal, not from its speaking or even from my hearing it, but from its merely being seen, so that, after seeing it with my own eyes, I may possess a self-sufficient and adequate verdict, from its mere appearance, that it exists. Then the obscure words belonging to hearing will no longer be able to overturn what belongs peculiarly to the eyes.

Nevertheless, I put this very consideration before a philosopher of my acquaintance, who advised me on many grounds not to dare such a thing. “For if the soul does not heed the magician,” he said, “you will live with a guilty conscience because you acted against the laws that forbid people to do these things. But if it does heed him, then, besides your living with a guilty conscience, I think that the concerns of piety will no longer prosper for you, though it was for this very purpose that you dared it. For they say that the divine is hostile to those who harass souls when dead bodies are dissolved.” When I heard this, I became more hesitant to attempt such a thing, but I did not abandon the plan I had formed from the beginning. Rather, as one whose impulse had been obstructed, I was disheartened.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀναπομπὴν (τὴν λεγομένην νεκρομαντείαν)","chosen":"summon up a soul—the practice called necromancy","rationale":"ἀναπομπή denotes a sending or bringing upward; “summon up” gives the contextual necromantic sense while retaining the upward movement."},{"source_quote":"αὐτάρκη καὶ ἱκανὴν ἀπόφασιν","chosen":"a self-sufficient and adequate verdict","rationale":"Retains both coordinated adjectives and renders ἀπόφασις as a settled determination rather than merely an informal opinion."},{"source_quote":"τὰ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ἴδια","chosen":"what belongs peculiarly to the eyes","rationale":"Preserves the contrast between the eyes’ own evidence and the obscure verbal evidence of hearing."},{"source_quote":"δυσσυνειδήτως βιώσεις","chosen":"you will live with a guilty conscience","rationale":"The adverb describes living under an adversely burdened conscience."},{"source_quote":"τῇ λύσει θανόντων σωμάτων","chosen":"when dead bodies are dissolved","rationale":"λύσις denotes loosening or dissolution; the rendering preserves its connection with bodily death without importing a more specific anthropology."},{"source_quote":"ὀκνηρότερος","chosen":"more hesitant","rationale":"In this context the comparative indicates increased reluctance to undertake the proposed act."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"1.6","text":"And, so that I may not recount such things to you at great length, while I was amid so many thoughts and affairs, a report arose quietly during the reign of Tiberius Caesar. Taking its beginning from the spring equinox, it kept growing from time to time and, like a truly good messenger from God, traveled throughout the world, unable to conceal God’s will in silence. Each time, therefore, it became more widespread and greater, saying that a certain man in Judea, having begun at the spring equinox, was proclaiming to the Jews the kingdom of the eternal God, which he said any one of them would enjoy if he first set his way of life right. And so that he might be believed—that, being full of divinity, he was doing these things—he performed many marvelous signs and wonders by command alone, as one who had received the authority from God. For he makes the deaf hear and the blind regain their sight; he makes people with deformed limbs walk and raises the lame upright; he drives away every disease and puts every demon to flight. Even lepers and those with scabies are healed and depart merely by looking intently at him from a distance. The dead are raised when brought to him, and there is nothing that he is unable to do.

Indeed, the more time advanced, the more what grew much greater and became more firmly established through increasing numbers of visitors was no longer the report, I mean, but the truth of the matter. For by then gatherings were even being held in various places for deliberation and inquiry into who the one who had appeared might be and what he intended to say.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἐξ ἐαρινῆς τροπῆς","chosen":"from the spring equinox","rationale":"The seasonal τροπή is understood as the spring turning point, conventionally the equinox."},{"source_quote":"ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθὴ θεοῦ ἄγγελος","chosen":"like a truly good messenger from God","rationale":"The report is personified as an ἄγγελος; “messenger” preserves the role without necessarily making the report a celestial being."},{"source_quote":"προκατορθώσῃ τὴν πολιτείαν","chosen":"first set his way of life right","rationale":"προκατορθόω conveys prior rectification, while πολιτεία here concerns conduct or manner of life."},{"source_quote":"θειότητος γέμων","chosen":"full of divinity","rationale":"Preserves the abstract noun θεότης and the image of being filled with it."},{"source_quote":"κυλλοὺς ποιεῖ περιπατεῖν, χωλοὺς ἀνορθοῖ","chosen":"he makes people with deformed limbs walk and raises the lame upright","rationale":"Uses distinct expressions for κυλλοί and χωλοί rather than collapsing the two clauses into a single reference to lameness."},{"source_quote":"λεπροὶ ψωροὶ","chosen":"lepers and those with scabies","rationale":"Renders the asyndetic disease terms as distinguishable descriptions, with ψωροί referring to an itching or scabby skin condition."},{"source_quote":"συστήματα κατὰ τόπους","chosen":"gatherings were even being held in various places","rationale":"σύστημα denotes an organized gathering or assembly, and κατὰ τόπους distributes these gatherings across locations."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"τὴν. τοῦ ἀιδίου θεοῦ","issue":"The printed full stop separates the article from its dependent genitive phrase, although the syntax requires them to be read continuously. The translation does not treat the stop as a sentence boundary.","proposed_reading":"τὴν τοῦ ἀιδίου θεοῦ","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"1.7","text":"Then, at one point in that same year, at the autumn equinox, someone stood publicly and cried out, saying, “Romans, listen! The Son of God is present in Judea, promising eternal life to all who desire it, if they live in accordance with the will of the Father who sent him. Therefore change your way from worse things to better, from temporary things to eternal. Know that there is one God, the heavenly one, whose world you inhabit unjustly before his righteous eyes. But if you change and live according to his will, then, after being carried into another age and becoming everlasting, you will enjoy his inexpressible good things. If, however, you disobey, your souls, after the dissolution of the body, will be cast into the place of fire, where, being punished everlastingly, they will reorient themselves to no avail. For the present life of each person is the time for reorientation.”

When I heard these things, I was distressed that no one from among so many crowds, after hearing so momentous an announcement, had said, “I will travel to Judea so that I may see whether this man is speaking the truth when he says these things.” For the Son of God had come to Judea, revealing the will of the Father who sent him for the sake of a good and eternal hope, especially since what they say he proclaims is no small matter. For he firmly declares that some people’s souls, being eternal, will enjoy eternal good things, whereas the souls of others, after being cast into unquenchable fire, will be punished forever.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἐν φθινοπωρινῇ τροπῇ","chosen":"at the autumn equinox","rationale":"As in the preceding reference to the spring τροπή, the seasonal turning point is understood as the equinox."},{"source_quote":"μεταβάλλεσθε τὸν τρόπον","chosen":"change your way","rationale":"The verb is μεταβάλλω, not μετανοέω, and the object τὸν τρόπον identifies the person’s manner or way of life."},{"source_quote":"ἀπὸ τῶν προσκαίρων ἐπὶ τὰ αἰώνια","chosen":"from temporary things to eternal","rationale":"Preserves the substantival contrast between what lasts only for a time and what is eternal."},{"source_quote":"τῶν ἀπορρήτων αὐτοῦ ἀγαθῶν","chosen":"his inexpressible good things","rationale":"ἀπόρρητος can describe what is not to be spoken or cannot be expressed; “inexpressible” fits the promised divine benefits."},{"source_quote":"ἀνωφέλητα μετανοήσουσιν","chosen":"they will reorient themselves to no avail","rationale":"Applies the supplied terminology for μετανοέω while preserving the explicit claim that this postmortem reorientation is ineffective."},{"source_quote":"ὁ γὰρ τῆς μετανοίας καιρὸς","chosen":"the time for reorientation","rationale":"Uses the corresponding policy rendering for μετάνοια without adding a destination absent from the Greek."},{"source_quote":"τὸν αἰῶνα κολασθήσεσθαι","chosen":"will be punished forever","rationale":"Here the accusative expression denotes punishment continuing through the age, idiomatically represented as “forever.”"}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"σώματος·λύσιν","issue":"The printed medial stop falls between the dependent genitive σώματος and λύσιν. The translation reads the phrase continuously.","proposed_reading":"σώματος λύσιν","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ὡς ὅτι υἱὸς θεοῦ ἐπιδεδήμηκεν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ","issue":"The discourse force of the sequence ὡς ὅτι is uncertain. The translation takes it as introducing an explanatory assertion, “For the Son of God had come,” rather than silently altering the supplied wording.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":true}]},{"reference":"1.8","text":"As I said these things about others, I also addressed myself, saying, “Why do I blame others when I am under the same charge of negligence? No, I will set out for Judea, after first putting my life in order.” Yet, after I had resolved on this course, a long period of delay followed, because the affairs of life were difficult to break free from.

At last, then, I reflected in this way on the nature of life: by entangling those who are eager to act in hope, it lies in wait for them. I also considered how much time I had somehow been drawn in unawares, tossed about by hopes, and that, while occupied in this way, we human beings die. Leaving everything of mine just as it happened to be, I set out for Portus. After reaching the harbor and putting out to sea, I was carried by the hostility of the winds to Alexandria instead of Judea. Then, detained there by a lack of winds, I associated with the philosophers and recounted the reports concerning the rumor and the man who had appeared in Rome. They answered, “We do not know the man who appeared in Rome. But about the one who arose in Judea and whom the rumor calls the Son of God, we too have heard from many who came from there, and we have learned about all the wonders he performed as he spoke.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"πρότερον τὸν ἐμὸν διαθεὶς βίον","chosen":"after first putting my life in order","rationale":"διατίθημι here indicates arranging or settling one’s life and affairs before departure."},{"source_quote":"τῶν βιωτικῶν πραγμάτων δυσεκλύτων ὄντων","chosen":"because the affairs of life were difficult to break free from","rationale":"The rendering preserves both the practical affairs denoted by βιωτικά and the difficulty of disengagement expressed by δυσεκλύτων."},{"source_quote":"ἐλπίδι ἐμπλέκων τοὺς σπεύδοντας ἐνεδρεύει","chosen":"by entangling those who are eager to act in hope, it lies in wait for them","rationale":"Retains the paired images of entanglement and ambush used to characterize life."},{"source_quote":"τὰ πάντα μου ὡς ἔτυχεν ἀφεὶς","chosen":"leaving everything of mine just as it happened to be","rationale":"Preserves the sense that Clement departed without first bringing his possessions or affairs into an orderly condition."},{"source_quote":"εἰς Πόρτον","chosen":"for Portus","rationale":"Πόρτος is treated as the proper name of the port settlement rather than translated generically."},{"source_quote":"ἀνέμων ἔχθραις","chosen":"by the hostility of the winds","rationale":"Retains the source’s personifying image rather than reducing it to merely adverse weather."},{"source_quote":"ἀνέμων ἀπορίᾳ","chosen":"by a lack of winds","rationale":"ἀπορία here indicates a deficiency or absence of wind that prevents onward sailing."},{"source_quote":"περὶ πάντων ὧν λαλῶν ἐποίει θαυμασίων","chosen":"about all the wonders he performed as he spoke","rationale":"The circumstantial participle may suggest performance by speech or contemporaneously with speech; “as he spoke” preserves that ambiguity."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ. ὃν ποτε","issue":"The printed full stop interrupts the correlative expression οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καί and separates it from the further object of reflection. The translation reads the construction continuously.","proposed_reading":"οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ ὃν ποτε","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ὃν ποτε εἰσεκλάπην χρόνον ἐλπίσιν δονούμενος","issue":"The construction is semantically difficult, especially the force of εἰσεκλάπην with the accusative of time. The translation understands Clement as having been drawn or ensnared unawares for a length of time while hopes tossed him about, but the precise nuance remains uncertain.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":true}]}]}
